title: The Region of Convergence
intro: The formula X(z) is only half of a z-transform. The other half is the region where the sum behind it converges, and two different signals can share one formula and differ only there.

blocks.text: The region of convergence is the set of $z$ for which $\sum_n |x[n]\, z^{-n}| < \infty$. As the z-Plane (#/math/z-transform/z-plane) page showed, that depends only on $|z|$, so the ROC is a ring $r_{in} < |z| < r_{out}$, where $r_{in}$ may be 0 and $r_{out}$ may be $\infty$. Four rules fix it for a rational transform:

items: The ROC contains no poles: at a pole $X(z)$ is infinite, so the sum cannot converge there.
It is bounded by poles (or reaches 0 or infinity): its inner and outer circles pass through a pole, or there is no edge.
A right-sided signal (zero before some time $n_0$) has an ROC outside its outermost pole: $|z| > \max_k |p_k|$. It includes $\infty$ if the signal is also causal ($n_0 \ge 0$).
A left-sided signal (zero after some time) has an ROC inside its innermost pole: $|z| < \min_k |p_k|$. A two-sided signal has a ring between two poles, or no ROC at all.

blocks.text: A finite-length signal is a special case: its sum has finitely many terms, so it converges everywhere except possibly at $z = 0$ (if it has samples at $n > 0$, which put $z^{-n}$ in the sum) and at $z = \infty$ (if it has samples at $n < 0$).
The right-sided exponential $a^n u[n]$ has $X(z) = z/(z - a)$ for $|z| > |a|$. The left-sided signal $-a^n u[-n-1]$, which is $-a^n$ for $n \le -1$ and 0 from $n = 0$ on, gives

The same formula, with the opposite region. The surface drawn by the formula is the same in both cases; what changes is which part of it is real. In the viewer below the left-sided signal is solid inside the circle $|z| = 0.8$ and faded outside. Switch Input signal to decaying exponential rⁿu[n] and the shading flips: the same landscape, the other part of it now solid.
This is why an inverse z-transform needs the ROC as well as the formula. Without it, $z/(z - 0.8)$ could be a signal that decays toward $n = +\infty$ or one that blows up toward $n = -\infty$.

$x[n] = r^{|n|}$ with $0 < r < 1$ decays in both directions. Its right half $r^n u[n]$ needs $|z| > r$; its left half, $r^{-n}$ for $n \le -1$, needs $|z| < 1/r$. Both hold in the ring $r < |z| < 1/r$, and there

blocks.tex: X(z) = \frac{z}{z - r} + \frac{r z}{1 - r z} = \frac{(1 - r^2)\, z}{(z - r)(1 - r z)}, \qquad r < |z| < \frac{1}{r}

blocks.text: Poles at $r$ and $1/r$, mirror images through the unit circle, with the ROC the ring between them. With $r = 0.5$ the ring is $0.5 < |z| < 2$ and contains the unit circle. Push Radius r to 1 or beyond and the ring closes: the viewer says there is no ROC and fades the whole surface, because $r^{|n|}$ no longer decays in either direction.
Why it matters: stability and causality
When $x[n]$ is the impulse response $h[n]$ of a system, the ROC answers two questions at a glance:

items: Causal (the output never depends on future input): $h[n] = 0$ for $n < 0$, so the ROC is the outside of a circle and includes $\infty$.
Stable in the bounded-input, bounded-output (BIBO) sense: $\sum_n |h[n]| < \infty$, which is the same as saying the unit circle lies inside the ROC.
Both: the ROC is outside the outermost pole and contains the unit circle, so every pole is inside the unit circle.

blocks.text: The Pole Positions (#/math/z-transform/poles-and-time) page works through what the poles do to the signal itself.

blocks.title: Three ROCs, one formula
blocks.text: $X(z) = \dfrac{1}{(1 - 0.5z^{-1})(1 - 2z^{-1})}$. List every possible ROC and say which one gives a stable signal and which a causal one.
solution: Poles at $0.5$ and $2$. The possible rings are $|z| < 0.5$, $0.5 < |z| < 2$ and $|z| > 2$.
Only the middle ring contains the unit circle, so only it is stable; that signal is two-sided. $|z| > 2$ is causal but unstable, and $|z| < 0.5$ is left-sided and unstable.
blocks.answer: Stable: $0.5 < |z| < 2$. Causal: $|z| > 2$. No ROC is both.

blocks.title: A finite signal
solution: $X(z) = z + 1 + z^{-1}$. The term $z$ is infinite at $z = \infty$ and $z^{-1}$ is infinite at $z = 0$; everything else is finite, so the ROC is $0 < |z| < \infty$.
